facts.text: Salem was founded in 1675 by Quaker John Fenwick, making it New Jersey's oldest continuously inhabited European‑settled city.
The Friends Meeting House, built in 1736, stands as a well‑preserved example of early Quaker architecture in Salem.
Salem’s location on the Delaware River shaped its maritime heritage, with river trade influencing the city’s development for centuries.
In 1798, Salem was incorporated as one of New Jersey’s original 104 townships, cementing its role in the state’s early governance.
The Glass House Spur of the Salem Branch, a 1.2‑mile rail line, connects the Port of Salem to regional freight networks.
Salem’s name derives from the Hebrew word “shalom,” meaning peace, reflecting the founders’ desire for a harmonious community.
